extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political theory, and comparative anthropology; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: An analytical essay comparing the structural and functional organization of societies to biological organisms, and an inquiry into the origins of animal/plant worship (totemism) among primitive peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation into governing and governed classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary differentiation of societies into the governing and governed classes, analogous to the differentiation of tissues (ectoderm etc.) which develop into organs of external action and organs of alimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that as societies evolve they develop a superior class transformed into the directive-executive system (legislative and defensive appliances). The text draws the biological analogy (ectoderm → nerve-muscular system) to justify expecting specialized social strata with capacities required for higher social functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of rulers change with societal complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: In rude assemblages the strongest, most courageous, and most sagacious become rulers; in more advanced societies the rulers tend to be those of greatest cunning, foresight, and skill in managing others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion for understanding leadership selection across stages of social development: physical strength and daring characterize early chiefs; as directive duties accumulate, mental qualities (cunning, foresight, management skill) become decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of directive and executive functions
rubrics_metrics.description: As social duties accumulate, the chief confines himself more to directing public affairs and deputes execution to others; directive and executive agencies grow distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the transition: head chiefs stop personally administering justice or enforcing obedience, instead delegating coercive and administrative acts—an emergent division of labor analogous to separation of nervous centres and muscles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of advising bodies/ministry (ganglion analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: As rulers gather advisers who communicate information, prepare subjects, and issue orders, a group of governing units forms comparable to a ganglion consisting of many cells; advisers begin to exercise control over the ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that advisers/ministerial bodies sway the ruler's judgment and can make him an automatic centre reflecting external impressions. This is a standard for interpreting ministerial influence and the emergence of collective directive organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization and subordination of local rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: With increased commercial and governmental union, minor rulers fall under the control of a chief directive centre and become agents administering the supreme ruler's laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to local ganglia becoming subordinate to a cephalic ganglion; used as an explanatory criterion for political consolidation and the reduction of local independence during state formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament as averaging the interests of classes; 'good Parliament' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The office of a Parliament is described as that of averaging the interests of the various classes in a community; a good Parliament balances party interests so that united legislation allows to each class as much as is consistent with the claims of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit evaluative standard: legislative bodies should interpret and combine varied class-impressions and produce laws harmonious with general wants, analogous to the brain 'averaging' physical, intellectual, and moral interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative bodies operate via representations, not direct impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative consciousness: large governing masses (like the cerebrum) deal with representations of impressions rather than direct sensations; Parliament is a representative body because interests are represented to it by members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames debate as conflict of representations of consequences; implies a standard for structuring representative institutions (i.e., they must process indirect information through organised representation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division between legislative decision and executive fulfillment
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative decisions do not themselves carry out actions; fulfilment devolves on executive organs (Parliament → Ministers → King), in analogy to cerebrum decisions being executed by subjacent ganglia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies institutional roles: directive bodies decide and subordinate executive divisions implement—useful for evaluating institutional design and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency executive action with retrospective deliberative review
rubrics_metrics.description: On national emergencies requiring prompt action, executive centres (King and Ministry) may issue commands without laying matters before deliberative bodies; the deliberative powers later discuss and may grant or withhold indemnity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets an operational standard for exceptional executive prerogative: swift executive action can be legitimate if followed by subsequent deliberative review and approval or condemnation (analogy to involuntary spinal reflexes followed by contemplation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for an internuncial apparatus / communication channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex societies require an 'internuncial apparatus'—channels analogous to nerves (e.g., telegraph-wires) through which directive centres receive information and convey commands efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the parallel with nerve-bundles and arteries, and notes practical analogies (telegraph along railways, a regulating wire akin to the sympathetic nerve to control traffic). Use as a criterion for assessing societal coordination: the presence and organization of communication infrastructure is essential to complex governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good central organ principle: balance of diverse interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good brain' (by analogy a good central governing body) is one in which the desires answering to physical, intellectual, and moral interests are so balanced that the conduct they jointly dictate sacrifices none of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General normative standard for central decision-making: balance competing categories of interest so policy does not unduly sacrifice one class of goods for another; applied explicitly to assess parliaments and governing organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for acceptable explanation of animal/plant worship (totemism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any satisfactory explanation for the widespread worship of animals and plants among primitive peoples must be general (not rely on exceptional local causes), consistent with the cognitive capacities and limited verbal symbols of primitive men, and explain repeated independent occurrence worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author rejects ad hoc or exceptional causes and proposes mechanisms grounded in ordinary human experience—shadows, reflections in water, echoes, dreams, fainting, epilepsy, somnambulism and other abnormalities of consciousness—that plausibly lead to belief in a double self and hence ancestor-propitiation which can evolve into totemism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism: descent of nicknames leading to tribal totems
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals habitually acquire nicknames suggestive of personal traits or associations with animals/plants/objects; such nicknames can be inherited by descendants and perpetuated by dominant families, eventually becoming the name and totem of a tribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples are provided (e.g., an ancestor called 'the Wolf' whose descendants and followers keep the name, forming 'the Wolves'; Scottish example 'Croshek' as a local nickname). Use as an explanatory criterion for how personal metaphorical naming can crystallize into collective totemic identity.
